stat-card.what: A small panel that shows one key number with a label and often a comparison, such as the change since last week. It lets people check a metric at a glance.
uses: Showing headline figures at the top of a dashboard.
Summarising totals, rates or durations on an overview page.
Linking a key number to the detailed report behind it.
avoid: Comparing many values across categories; use a table or chart instead.
Long explanations; put them in text beside the number.
practices: Make the number the largest thing on the card.
Put the label and the comparison period right next to the number.
Show units and the direction of change in words or symbols, not colour alone.
Limit a row to a handful of cards so each one stands out.

key-value-list.what: A list of labelled facts about one item, with each name paired with its value. It makes the properties of a record quick to scan.
uses: Showing the details of a record on a detail page.
Summarising an order, account or device in a side panel.
Reviewing entered information before confirming.
avoid: Comparing the same fields across many records; use a table.
Long descriptive text; use normal paragraphs.
practices: Keep labels short and consistent in wording.
Align labels and values so the eye follows one edge.
Show a clear 'Not set' instead of leaving a value blank.
Stack labels above values on narrow screens.

list.what: A vertical set of related items shown as rows, each with a title and sometimes an image or extra detail. It is the simplest way to show a short collection.
uses: Recent activity, files or members in a side panel.
Search results or notifications.
Menus of options that need a description for each choice.
avoid: Comparing several attributes of many items; use a table.
Very long collections without paging or search; add paging, search or filters.
practices: Give every row the same structure so it reads the same way.
Make the whole row clickable when it opens something.
Separate rows with thin lines or spacing, not heavy boxes.
Keep the most important text first in each row.

list-item.what: A single row in a list, usually with a small visual, a title, a short description and a detail on the right. It can be plain, clickable or selected.
uses: Rows in a list of people, files or messages.
Options in a menu that need a short description.
Highlighting the current choice in a list of places or items.
avoid: Dense data with many columns; use a table row.
A group of unrelated actions; use buttons or a menu.
practices: Keep rows to about one or two lines of text.
Make the click target the full width of the row.
Show the selected item with more than colour, such as a check mark.
Place the same kind of information in the same spot on every row.

timeline-item.what: One event on a vertical timeline, shown with a marker, a title, a time and a short description. Stacked together, the items tell a story in order.
uses: Showing the history of an order, case or record.
Listing the steps and results of a process run.
Displaying an incident or activity log.
avoid: Comparing durations or overlaps between tasks; use a Gantt chart.
A handful of unordered facts; use a plain list.
practices: Always show a time or date for each event.
Order entries consistently: newest first for logs, oldest first for processes.
Use marker colour to signal event type, with words too.
Keep descriptions to a line or two.

sortable-header.what: A table column heading that people can select to sort the rows by that column. An arrow shows which column is sorted and in which direction.
uses: Ordering a table by name, date, count or status.
Finding the highest or lowest values in a column.
Letting people reorder search or report results.
avoid: Short tables of a few rows; sorting adds clutter.
Columns with no natural order, such as free-form notes.
practices: Show the current sort direction with an arrow and a text-based state for assistive technology.
Sort numbers and dates from highest to latest first by default.
Make only the useful columns sortable.
Keep filters and page position when the sort changes.

legend-item.what: A small colour swatch beside a name that explains what a colour or line in a chart or map stands for. Together the items form a legend.
uses: Naming each series in a multi-series chart.
Explaining colours on a map or diagram.
Showing values next to each category in a chart summary.
avoid: Single-series charts; a clear title is enough.
Charts with just a few points; label the points directly.
practices: Use the same colour and shape in the legend as in the chart.
Place the legend close to the chart.
Do not rely on colour alone; add shapes, patterns or direct labels.
Keep names short and in the same order as the chart.

zone-row.what: A row in a list of areas drawn on a video or image, showing the area's colour, name, type, count and actions. It ties the list to the shapes on screen.
uses: Listing the counting areas of a camera view.
Managing regions drawn on a map or floor plan.
Showing a count for each named area.
avoid: Generic lists of records; use a standard list item.
Comparing many numbers per area; use a table.
practices: Match the row's colour to the area shown on the image.
State the area type in words, not just by colour or pattern.
Align counts to the right with consistent number formatting.
Give each action a clear accessible name that includes the area.

line-count-item.what: A row that shows how many people or objects crossed a line in each direction, with arrows for the two directions. It reports counts for each line.
uses: Counting people entering and leaving a door.
Reporting vehicles crossing a road line.
Comparing in and out totals for each entrance.
avoid: Counts for areas rather than lines; use an area or zone summary.
Trends over time; use a chart.
practices: Show direction with arrows and words, not colour alone.
Use aligned digits so numbers line up in a list.
Label each line with a meaningful name.
Keep the same order of in and out on every row.

media-object.what: An image, avatar or icon placed beside a block of text. The picture helps people recognise the item before they read.
uses: Comments and messages with the author's avatar.
Search results or product summaries with a thumbnail.
Notifications with an icon and short text.
avoid: Large hero images; use a card with a full-width image.
Text-only content; use a plain list.
practices: Keep the image size the same across items.
Give the image empty alt text when the text already names the thing.
Align the picture to the top or centre consistently.
Keep the text short enough to avoid wrapping around the picture.

card.what: A bordered container that groups the information and actions about one item, such as an image, a title, details and a footer. Cards sit well in grids.
uses: Browsing collections such as products, projects or reports.
Summarising an item with a picture and key facts.
Presenting a set of options side by side.
avoid: Wrapping every section of a page; use spacing and headings.
Comparing many attributes across items; use a table.
practices: Make each card about one thing.
Keep the same content order on every card in a set.
Give the title the most visual weight.
Keep cards in a grid the same height and width for easy scanning.

card-footer.what: The bottom strip of a card that holds its status and its actions. Keeping them in one place makes every card behave the same way.
uses: Showing an item's status, such as online or draft.
Adding one or two quick actions to a card.
Holding a small menu of more actions.
avoid: Many actions on a card; move them to the item's own page.
Essential content; keep that in the card body.
practices: Put the status on the left and actions on the right.
Limit actions to one or two so the footer stays clear.
Use clear labels or accessible names for icon buttons.
Keep the footer in the same position on all cards.

linked-card.what: A card where the whole area can be clicked to open the item it describes. It gives people a large target while exposing just one link to assistive technology.
uses: Cards that open a detail page, such as articles or projects.
Grids of places, products or reports.
Mobile-friendly lists where a big tap target helps.
avoid: Cards with several equal actions; use a normal card with buttons.
Cards that contain other links; nesting links causes errors.
practices: Put one clear link on the card's title.
Never place a link inside another link.
Keep secondary controls reachable and above the main link area.
Show a clear hover and focus state across the whole card.

accordion.what: A stack of headings that each open and close a section of content. People see all topics first and open only what they need.
uses: Frequently asked questions.
Advanced settings or optional details.
Long pages with grouped information, especially on small screens.
avoid: Content most people need; show it directly.
Sequential steps in a process; use a step indicator.
Navigation between pages; use a menu.
practices: Write headings as the topic or question people look for.
Use a clear marker, such as an arrow, to show it can open.
Allow several sections to be open at once.
Keep panel content short and focused.

steps.what: A row or column of numbered stages that shows how far someone has got in a multi-step task. Done, current and upcoming steps look different.
uses: Setup or onboarding flows.
Multi-page forms such as checkout.
Showing progress in a process with a fixed order.
avoid: Tasks with one or two steps; just do the task.
Free-order sections; use tabs or an accordion.
practices: Keep to about three to six steps.
Name each step with a short verb or noun phrase.
Show done, current and upcoming states with text or icons, not colour alone.
Let people go back to completed steps.

tree.what: A hierarchy of items that people can expand and collapse, like folders within folders. It shows structure and hides depth until needed.
uses: Browsing folders, locations or categories.
Showing an organisation or site structure.
Choosing an item from nested groups.
avoid: Flat lists; use a plain list.
Main site navigation with only a few levels; use a menu.
practices: Indent child items clearly.
Support keyboard use with arrow keys and Enter.
Show counts or hints on branches so people know what is inside.
Mark the current item and keep it visible.

avatar-group.what: A cluster of overlapping profile pictures showing the people involved with something, with a count for the rest. It shows who is involved without listing everyone.
uses: Showing assignees or participants on a task card.
Displaying members of a team or project.
Showing who is attending an event.
avoid: When people need to see every name; use a full list.
Showing a single person; use one avatar with the name.
practices: Show only a few avatars and a '+N' count for the rest.
Give each person a text name for assistive technology.
Link the group to the full list of people.
Keep avatar sizes the same and overlap small enough to see each face.

table-card.what: A framed panel that holds a titled table together with its actions and page controls. The frame tells people what the rows are before they read them.
uses: Showing a top-ten or recent-items table on a dashboard.
Listing related records on a detail page.
Giving a table its own title, description and links.
avoid: A table with no title or context; a plain table may be enough.
A table you can't use on a phone; use a list or cards.
practices: Give the table a clear title and a short description.
Right-align numbers and keep units in the column heading.
Put page controls and actions close to the table.
Show a helpful message when there is no data.

property-row.what: A row with an editable name and value and a remove button, repeated so people can add their own custom fields. It handles lists that vary in length.
uses: Editing custom properties or labels.
Adding request headers or environment values.
Entering metadata with no fixed set of fields.
avoid: Known fixed fields; use ordinary form fields.
Choosing from a set of allowed values; use select or checkboxes.
practices: Give an Add button that is easy to find and clear.
Name each remove button after the row, such as 'Remove property site-code'.
Label both fields, even if the labels repeat.
Check for empty or duplicate names before saving.

activity-entry.what: One line in a change history that states what happened, who did it, when, and how a value changed. It builds trust by showing who changed what.
uses: Audit logs for shared records.
History tabs on a record or setting.
Activity feeds of recent changes by a team.
avoid: Real-time chat or comments; use a conversation layout.
Long-term reporting; use a report with filters.
practices: Show who made the change and when.
Show old and new values side by side.
Use exact times in logs and relative times in feeds.
Keep entries short and consistent in structure.

carousel.what: A set of items shown one at a time with controls to move forward and back. It fits several related images into a small space.
uses: Photo galleries for a product or event.
Browsing a short series of related snapshots.
Showing screenshots in a small area on phones.
avoid: Important content people must not miss; show it on the page.
Long collections; use a grid or list.
practices: Show previous and next buttons plus a position count.
Do not advance slides automatically.
Give every image its own text description.
Support swiping on touch and arrow keys on keyboards.

scroller.what: A horizontal row of items that scrolls sideways and snaps into place, with part of the next item showing. The partly visible item hints that there is more.
uses: Rows of cards on phones.
Quick filters or tags in a single line.
Recently viewed items.
avoid: Content people must see in full; use a wrapped grid.
Long lists to scan or compare; use a vertical list.
practices: Let the next item peek into view to signal more.
Make the row reachable and scrollable by keyboard.
Snap to items so none stops half way.
Do not hide essential actions off-screen.

sparkline.what: A very small line chart with no axes that shows how a value has changed over time. It adds trend context to a number.
uses: Showing a trend next to a key number.
Adding a small chart in a table cell.
Summarising many series in a compact overview.
avoid: When exact values matter; use a full chart with axes.
Comparing many categories; use a bar chart.
practices: Pair it with the number it summarises.
Add a short text description for screen readers.
Mark the latest value, for example with a dot.
Keep the scale and time span the same across a set of rows.

donut-chart.what: A ring split into segments that shows how parts make up a whole, with the total often in the middle. It works best with only a few parts.
uses: Showing a share of visitors by source.
Showing a status breakdown of alerts or tasks.
Displaying how a total divides between a few categories.
avoid: More than about five parts; use a bar chart.
Comparing similar-sized shares precisely; use bars.
Showing change over time; use a line chart.
practices: Limit the ring to two to five segments.
Add a legend with names and exact values.
Do not rely on colour alone to tell segments apart.
Show the total in the centre.

chart-frame.what: A consistent wrapper around a chart that gives it a title, subtitle, legend, source note and a text version of its data. It helps people read and trust the chart.
uses: Wrapping any chart on a dashboard or report.
Adding units, source and time zone to a chart.
Offering the chart's data as a table for exact values.
avoid: Decorative images with no data; use a plain figure.
A single number; use a stat card.
practices: State what is measured, the unit and the period in the title or subtitle.
Reserve the chart's space so the page does not jump while it loads.
Name the source and update time.
Offer the data as a table for those who cannot read the chart.

dashboard.what: An overview page that gathers key numbers, charts and lists in one view so people can see how things are going at a glance.
uses: The home screen of an analytics or admin tool.
A team or site overview for managers.
Monitoring key figures over a chosen period.
avoid: Detailed work on single records; use detail or list pages.
Dense data exploration; use a report or table with filters.
practices: Put the most important numbers at the top.
State the time period the figures cover.
Keep to a few charts, each answering one question.
Link each number to the detail behind it.

calendar-page.what: A full page for viewing events by month, week, day or agenda, with controls to move between dates and switch views.
uses: Event, booking or shift calendars.
Planning a team's schedule.
Finding free days at a glance.
avoid: A single date choice in a form; use a date picker.
Resource-by-time planning; use a scheduler.
practices: Offer Today, previous and next controls in the same place.
Show the current period clearly in the title.
Let people switch between month, week, day and agenda views.
Do not rely on colour alone to tell event types apart.

scheduler-page.what: A page that shows one day or week by resource, such as people, rooms or vehicles, with bookings placed along a time axis. It shows who is free and when.
uses: Dispatching staff or installers.
Booking rooms or equipment.
Planning vehicle use.
avoid: General event calendars; use a calendar page.
Tasks with dependencies; use a timeline.
practices: Put one row per resource with a clear name.
Show the hours along the top.
Make double bookings and gaps easy to see.
Keep date controls close to the grid.

planning-board-page.what: A page that shows work as columns of cards, one column per stage, which people drag between columns. It is often called a kanban board.
uses: Tracking tasks through stages such as to do, doing and done.
Managing a pipeline of requests or leads.
Team workflows with a few clear stages.
avoid: Date-driven plans; use a timeline or calendar.
Large sets of records to sort or search; use a table.
practices: Keep to a few stages with clear names.
Show a card's owner and due date at a glance.
Offer a keyboard-friendly alternative to dragging.
Show limits on work in progress and mark when one is exceeded.

timeline-page.what: A page that shows tasks as bars along a time scale, with progress, milestones and a line for today. It is also known as a Gantt chart.
uses: Project plans and roll-outs.
Installation or production schedules.
Seeing which tasks overlap or slip.
avoid: Simple ordered history; use a vertical timeline.
Planning by resource; use a scheduler.
practices: Draw a clear marker for today.
Show progress on each bar.
Label bars with text, not colour alone.
Allow zooming or scrolling when the plan is long.

booking-flow.what: A page that guides someone through booking a service or time slot in a short series of steps, with a summary that updates as they choose.
uses: Booking appointments or classes.
Reserving a time slot or table.
Short purchase-like processes.
avoid: Long applications; use a multi-page form with saved progress.
A single quick choice; use one form.
practices: Show all steps and where the person is.
Keep a running summary of the choices made.
Offer clear Back and Continue buttons.
End with a confirmation that shows what was booked.

event-editor-page.what: A full page for creating or changing an event, with the form beside helpful context such as conflicts and guests. It gives space for many details.
uses: Creating or editing events, shifts or bookings.
Checking for clashes before saving.
Inviting and reviewing attendees.
avoid: A quick one-field edit; use inline editing.
Simple confirmations; use a dialog.
practices: Show conflicts next to the form before people save.
Keep Delete apart from Save and ask for confirmation.
Offer a clear Cancel route back.
Group related fields, such as date and time, together.

simple-data-page.what: A page that lists records in a table, with summary counts, search and filters above it. It is the standard page for browsing and managing data.
uses: Lists of orders, tickets, alerts or users.
Operational screens where counts by status matter.
Pages for searching and filtering records.
avoid: Overview of key figures; use a dashboard.
Editing one record in depth; use a detail page.
practices: Show counts by status as quick filters.
Keep search easy to find.
Show which filters are active and how to clear them.
Show a helpful message when nothing matches.

label.what: A short text above or beside a form field that names what to enter. It tells people and assistive technology what the field is for.
uses: Naming every text field, select and text area.
Titling a group of options with a legend.
Giving a clear click target that focuses the field.
avoid: Using placeholder text as the only name; it disappears while typing.
Vague words like 'Info'; use specific names.
practices: Place the label above the field and keep it visible.
Use short nouns in sentence case.
Connect the label to its field in the code.
Avoid colons and unneeded words like 'Your'.

required-marker.what: A short note beside a label, such as '(required)' or '(optional)', that tells people whether they must fill in a field.
uses: Marking optional fields in a mostly required form.
Marking required fields in a mostly optional form.
Long or unfamiliar forms where both states help.
avoid: Using only a red asterisk; it can look like an error and may be missed.
A general 'all fields required' notice that people skip.
practices: Use words rather than symbols alone.
Mark whichever kind of field is rarer.
Also set the required attribute so assistive technology knows.
Keep the marker beside the label, not in the field.

help-text.what: A short hint placed with a field that explains what to enter, such as a format or where to find the value. It helps people get it right the first time.
uses: Showing the expected format, such as a date or address.
Explaining what a choice will cause.
Telling people where to find a number or code.
avoid: Repeating the label; cut it instead.
Long instructions; link to a help page.
Hiding essential information in a tooltip.
practices: Keep it to one or two short sentences.
Place it between the label and the field.
Link it to the field so screen readers read it.
Use it to prevent errors, not explain them afterwards.

error-text.what: A message beside a field that says what is wrong and how to fix it. It helps people correct a mistake and continue.
uses: Telling someone a value has the wrong format.
Pointing out a missing required answer.
Explaining why a value was rejected, such as a duplicate.
avoid: Vague messages like 'Invalid input'; say what is wrong.
Showing errors while someone is still typing their first answer; wait until they leave the field.
practices: Write one sentence: what is wrong and how to fix it.
Place it next to the field it belongs to.
Use an icon and words, not colour alone.
Link it to the field and mark the field as invalid.

help-icon.what: A small question-mark button that reveals extra explanation on demand. It keeps background information out of the way until someone wants it.
uses: Explaining a technical term or how a figure is calculated.
Giving extra context in a dense form or report.
Offering background that experts may want.
avoid: Essential instructions; show them as visible help text.
Hover-only tooltips; they fail on touch and for keyboard users.
practices: Open it with a click or tap, as well as the keyboard.
Give the button a name that says the topic.
Keep the explanation brief.
Place it right after the text it explains.

error-list.what: A summary at the top of a form that lists every problem and links to each field. It gives people one place to start fixing things.
uses: Showing several problems after a failed submit.
Reporting an error that applies to the whole form.
Helping screen reader users find all the problems.
avoid: A single field error; show a message beside the field.
Warnings or tips that do not block submitting; use inline messages.
practices: State the number of problems in the title.
Make each item a link to its field.
Move focus to the summary after a failed submit.
Repeat each message beside its field.
